narrative:
The model determined that you have an 84% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk of failure is so high, the law school decided to reject your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the second decile means you placed in the bottom 20% of your class that year, noticeably lower than the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and similarly pulled the outcome toward failure; again you stood at the second decile, well below the typical sixth-decile performance of students who were admitted.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 40, your score sits above the average of 37.2 among accepted students, which gave the model some reason to expect you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the clear academic-ranking concerns.

The school did not consider your gender, race, family income, undergraduate GPA, or planned full-time status in reaching this outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in any remaining law-school coursework. You may also want to retake the LSAT or explore schools that place less weight on early class rankings. Consider speaking with an admissions counselor about what specific improvements would make your profile competitive in a future cycle.
